title: Management: Everyday Manners
notes: Foundations course video for puppy and obedience owners (not reactivity). Claude drafted all narration from Tori's brief (Nov 24); the Google Doc is the source of truth. Build with LESSON=lesson-everyday.json.

beats.say: Hi, I’m Tori Ganino with Calling All Dogs. Welcome to Management: Everyday Manners.

scenes.heading: Where we're headed
scenes.visual_concept: Plan slide: What you'll learn, Why it matters.

beats.say: In this section, we’ll look at why management matters, how practice shapes your dog’s brain, and how to manage five everyday situations: greetings at the door, mealtime, jumping for things in your hands, pulling on walks, and barking at people.
Get this right, and the manners you teach will actually stick.

scenes.heading: Practice makes perfect
scenes.visual_concept: Tori's boxer picture; green chips for wanted habits, red chips for unwanted ones; callout.

beats.say: Every time your puppy or dog does something, they’re practicing it. And what gets practiced gets better.
That’s true for the things we love, like sitting politely or coming when called.
And it’s just as true for the things we don’t want, like jumping on guests, grabbing food off the counter, or pulling on the leash.
beats.onscreen: Jumping on guests, Counter surfing, Pulling on the leash

beats.say: Your dog isn’t being bad. They’re doing what works for them. And every time it works, they’re more likely to do it again.

scenes.heading: Building pathways
scenes.visual_concept: Brain picture: the old pathway in red; a path in the woods wears in; the new pathway in green.

beats.say: Here’s what’s happening in the brain. Every time your dog does a behavior, the neural pathway for it gets stronger.
beats.show: Brain picture; old pathway lights up.

beats.say: Think of a path in the woods. The first time, it’s barely visible. The more it’s walked, the easier it is to follow.
beats.show: Path in the woods wears in.

beats.say: Puppies are building these paths every single day. The ones they walk most become their habits.
beats.show: Row: the most walked paths become habits.

beats.say: So the goal is simple: keep your dog off the old path, and help them walk a new one.
beats.onscreen: Off the old path, onto a new one

scenes.heading: Management and training
scenes.visual_concept: Two cards: Management (prevents practice, tool chips), Training (builds the new behavior); banner.

beats.say: That’s where management comes in. Management means setting up your dog’s world so they can’t practice the behavior you don’t want.
A gate, a leash, a crate, a closed door, food put away. Simple things that prevent the rehearsal.
beats.onscreen: Gate, Leash, Crate, Closed door, Food put away

beats.say: Training is the other half. It teaches your dog what to do instead, and makes that choice worth it.
Management stops the old habit from getting stronger. Training builds the new one. You need both.

scenes.heading: The foundation
scenes.visual_concept: Tori's house: the foundation, floors build up (new behaviors), a crack opens and the house shifts; callout.

beats.say: Think of it like building a house. Management is the foundation. Training builds the floors on top of it.
Every new behavior you teach, like sitting at the door, waiting for the bowl, or walking on a loose leash, is another floor.
beats.onscreen: Sit at the door, Wait for the bowl, Loose leash walking

beats.say: But if the foundation has a crack, everything you build on it starts to shift. Every time your dog practices what you don’t want, that’s a crack.
Keep the foundation solid, and the new behaviors you teach will hold.

scenes.heading: Everyone follows the plan
scenes.visual_concept: Every time + Every person; red callout; four people cards.

beats.say: Management only works if everyone follows it, every time.
If one person lets the puppy jump up for a hug, or slips food from the table, your dog learns the rule is optional.
So get the whole household on the same page: family, kids, guests, dog walkers, and sitters.
beats.onscreen: Family, Kids, Guests, Walkers and sitters

scenes.heading: Greetings at the door
scenes.visual_concept: Situation slide: picture at right (golden jumping on a guest); Practicing / Manage it / Teach instead.

beats.say: Let’s start at the front door. A guest walks in, and your dog jumps all over them. If that happens again and again, jumping becomes the way your dog says hello.
To manage it, put up a baby gate or clip on a leash before you open the door, so your dog can’t reach your guest.
beats.onscreen: Baby gate or leash, before the door opens

beats.say: Then teach what you want instead, like four paws on the floor or going to a mat, and reward that calm hello.
beats.onscreen: Four paws on the floor, or go to a mat

scenes.heading: Mealtime
scenes.visual_concept: Situation slide: picture placeholder (mealtime); four red chips; Manage it rows; Teach instead.

beats.say: Next, food. Counter surfing, mugging you while you cook, jumping up while you make their meal, guarding the bowl. Every time it pays off, it gets stronger.
beats.onscreen: Counter surfing, Mugging, Jumping at meal prep, Guarding the bowl

beats.say: Manage it by keeping food off the counters and out of reach, and by using a gate, crate, or mat while you make meals and while you eat.
beats.onscreen: Food out of reach; gate, crate, or mat during meals

beats.say: If your dog guards the bowl, give them a quiet spot to eat in peace, with no one hovering or reaching in. If it’s getting worse, reach out for help.
beats.onscreen: A quiet spot to eat in peace

beats.say: Then teach a calm sit or wait. The bowl only goes down when your dog is calm.
beats.onscreen: Calm sit or wait; the bowl goes down when calm

scenes.heading: Jumping for things in hands
scenes.visual_concept: Situation slide: picture placeholder; Practicing / Manage it / Teach instead.

beats.say: Then there’s jumping up for whatever’s in your hands: food, toys, shoes, the mail. If jumping gets them the thing even once, they’ll try again, and harder.
beats.onscreen: Jumping for food, toys, shoes, the mail

beats.say: Manage it by keeping things up and out of reach, and using a leash or tether when people are carrying something your dog wants.
beats.onscreen: Out of reach; leash or tether

beats.say: Teach a sit or four paws on the floor instead. That calm choice is what earns the toy or the treat.
beats.onscreen: Sit or four paws on the floor earns it

scenes.heading: Pulling on walks
scenes.visual_concept: Situation slide: picture placeholder; Practicing / Manage it (harness, head halter conditioned) / Teach instead.

beats.say: On walks, every time your dog pulls and gets where they want to go, pulling works. Do that every day, and it becomes how they walk.
Manage it with a well fitted harness. A head halter can help too, as long as your dog has been properly conditioned to wear it.
While you’re training, keep walks shorter and calmer, so your dog isn’t practicing pulling for an hour every day.
beats.onscreen: Shorter, calmer walks while you train

beats.say: Then teach loose leash walking, and reward your dog for walking next to you.

scenes.heading: Barking at people
scenes.visual_concept: Situation slide: picture at right (golden barking at a man through the window); reasons; manage it; ABCs course card.

beats.say: And finally, barking at people, at the window or out on walks.
Dogs bark at people for different reasons. Sometimes they really want that person to come closer. And when the person comes over, or the barking gets attention, it works.
beats.onscreen: They want the person to come closer

beats.say: Manage it by blocking the view at the window, with film or closed blinds, and by giving people space on walks before your dog starts barking.
beats.onscreen: Block the view; give people space

beats.say: Why your dog barks matters, because it changes how we train. We cover that in our ABCs of Behavior course.

scenes.heading: “Just this once”
scenes.visual_concept: Just this once chips drop one by one, each adding a rep on the old path (red meter); callout.

beats.say: It’s easy to think, just this once won’t hurt. A quick jump for a hug, one bite from the table.
But your dog doesn’t know it’s just this once. To them, it’s one more rep on the old path.
beats.onscreen: One more rep on the old path

beats.say: Small slips add up. Being consistent is what makes new manners stick.

scenes.heading: Bringing it together
scenes.visual_concept: Level house on its foundation; three takeaways; closing statement; logo close.

beats.say: Let’s bring it together. What your dog practices, they get better at. Management keeps the unwanted behaviors from being practiced.
Training teaches what to do instead, and everyone in your home follows the same plan.
Management is the foundation. Build on it, and the manners you teach will last.
